name: Aisha Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Aisha, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say here is confidential. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you honestly think. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for Meridian Health Supply. We wholesale over-the-counter medicines, vitamins and first-aid products to about 300 independent pharmacies. I start by looking at my notebook, because I still keep a paper list of what's urgent. Then I check expiry dates and stock, ring the manufacturers' reps, and approve orders. Pharmacies hate running out of paracetamol, so I'm careful.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters. When a rural pharmacy needs a children's fever syrup and I find it, that's a good day. What wears me out is the constant pressure on price from the chains and the paperwork every time a rule changes. I'm 43, my husband Imran is an electrician working for himself, we have Sana and Hamza, and a mortgage that eats the first week of every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, I'm not surprised. At work I'd tell colleagues that whenever a new system arrives it takes six months to fix the mistakes. Among friends I'd shrug. I've heard big promises about computers my whole career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my job carries on, though not stress-free. Meridian is competing with two bigger wholesalers and margins are small. If a big pharmacy chain left us, I'd be worried, and that isn't about AI. Our savings are about two months, and Imran's income goes up and down with the season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. I'd do the same checks, ring the same reps, keep my notebook. I'd try to put a little more into savings each month, maybe 150, and I wouldn't change anything big. If management asked me to use one of the new ordering tools, I'd learn it slowly and check it twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in the ordinary way. It's not a crisis, but I'd be counting. When money's tight even small things, like Hamza's football club fees, make me stop and think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI tools. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I just don't see the point. I know how my own system works, and I trust my own eyes on an expiry date. If an error happens, someone's medicine isn't on the shelf. I can't hand that to something I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the first thing to feel tight in your household budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Imran's income. Electricians get quiet months in winter, and some months he earns half. Then the mortgage comes out of my wage alone, and we dip into the two months. That's the pressure even without any AI.

say: I'd tell colleagues new systems take **six months** to fix, and I've heard big promises before.
think: My job carries on, but **margins** are small and losing a big pharmacy chain would hurt.
Imran's **seasonal income** and two months of savings are the real pressure.
do: Keep the same checks, reps and **notebook**, and learn any new tool slowly.
Put about **150 more** a month into savings.
feel: **Uneasy** in the ordinary way, counting every small cost.
S0.quote: I know how my own system works, and I trust my own eyes on an expiry date.
fieldNote: Aisha's worry comes from **household money**: Imran's winter months and a mortgage that takes the first week's pay.
She rejects AI on **safety** grounds, since a wrong expiry date reaches patients.

steps.text: Keep ringing reps and checking expiry dates by eye
Learn any new ordering tool slowly and check it twice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should go slowly and test everything. At work I'd ask for written rules on what the software can and can't order. I'd tell my friends it's like any other change, some of it will stick and some won't. I wouldn't post anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it frightens me more than I let on. Stock checks, reorders and comparing prices are most of what I do before lunch, and a system can do them faster. They'll still need someone to check, but maybe one person instead of four. I'm average at this job, not a star, and I haven't picked up the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'm told, and I'd learn the new system because I'd have to, but I'd rather someone teaches me properly, in a class. I'd ask the manager what my job would be in two years. I'd also start quietly checking jobs in regulatory or compliance roles, because someone human has to sign off on medicines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. A bit like waiting for test results. I can't control it, so my stomach does the worrying for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks could software take on first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The reorders, definitely. I place about 60 a day, and most are routine. The things I'd keep are the odd ones, like a recall notice or a rep telling me a batch is delayed, where you have to decide quickly and talk to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your manager if your team got smaller?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I'm reliable and I know the pharmacies, and I'd like to be part of the new set-up. I'd ask for training before anything changes. And I'd ask if there's a role for someone who can sign off orders, because I would rather be that person than out of work.

say: We should **go slowly** and test everything, with written rules on what software can order.
think: Stock checks and reorders fill my morning, so **maybe one person** is needed instead of four.
I haven't learned the new tools, and I'm **average** at the job.
do: Ask my manager what my job is in two years and request **proper training** in a class.
Quietly look at **compliance** roles, since a human must sign off on medicines.
S1.quote: Stock checks, reorders and comparing prices are most of what I do before lunch, and a system can do them faster.
fieldNote: Aisha is more afraid than she shows, and **routine reorders** (about 60 a day) are the exposed part.
Her fallback is a **sign-off** role, which uses her caution as a strength.

steps.text: Ask the manager what my role is in two years
Request classroom training on the new ordering system
Look at compliance and sign-off roles in medicine supply

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, it's too fast and nobody asked us. At work I'd say we need a plan, and I'd want the government to be telling us what's coming. I wouldn't know what to put online. I'd probably just read what others write.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I lose my job and I don't know how to stop it. Everything I do at the desk is thinking work, and that's what arrives first. I'd have two months of savings and a mortgage. I'd say I have about a year before it gets ugly, and I wouldn't know where to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd freeze for a few weeks, honestly. Then I'd pull the budget apart, cut the club fees and eating out, and ask the bank what they'd allow. I'd ask my mother if we could count on her if it went bad. And I'd go to Imran's customers' network, see if there's work with his firm, even admin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like standing on a bridge in the fog. I'd do the school run and the cooking, and be somewhere else in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Imran talk about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Imran, I think my job is going in two years. He'd go very quiet, and then say we'd manage, like he always does. Then we'd sit at the kitchen table with paper and add up everything, because that's how we think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the robot delay matter for Imran's work and yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in one way. Imran's work is hands-on, wiring houses, so he's safe for longer, and that's the one thing keeping me going. But the kids' world is going to be strange, and I can't plan for it. I've never planned for something I can't see.

say: It's **too fast** and nobody asked us, and the government should tell us what's coming.
I wouldn't know what to post, so I'd just **read** what others write.
think: I think I lose my job and I don't know **how to stop it**.
I'd have two months saved, a mortgage, and about a **year** before it gets ugly.
do: Pull the budget apart, cut **club fees** and eating out, and ask the bank what they'd allow.
Ask my **mother** for help and see if Imran's firm has admin work.
feel: **Frightened**, like standing on a bridge in fog.
S2.quote: Everything I do at the desk is thinking work, and that's what arrives first.
fieldNote: Aisha expects her job to go and has **no ready plan**, and she says she'd freeze for a few weeks.
Imran's **hands-on trade** is the one thing she holds onto, which she says directly.

steps.text: Cut club fees and eating out within the first month
Ask the bank what payment relief they allow
Ask my mother to be a backup for childcare and bills
Ask about admin work at Imran's firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is better, but we still need a plan from somebody. At work I'd keep asking management what the company intends. I'd also tell friends to not wait, even though I know I might wait myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it gives me breathing room. I'd be 48 in 2031, Sana 18 and Hamza 15. I still believe my job goes, but with time I might find a path into something where people have to sign off, like regulation, quality control or training new staff. I'm not sure how, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd save harder, aim for six months in the bank. I'd ask Meridian to send me on a course for regulatory affairs, something recognised. I'd keep my head down and do my job well in case they keep the careful people. And I'd talk to Imran about whether he should take on an apprentice, since that work lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less scared than the two-year one, but a dull, heavy worry that sits there. It's like having a bill due in five years that I can't pay yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do that two wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be able to take a proper course, say evenings for a year, and still be home for the kids. In two years I'd have no time for that. But I know I might use the time to avoid it, and that's what I'm afraid of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about putting things off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd put it off, because I always do. I'd tell myself, there's time, and then it's year four and there's no savings and no course. I know that about myself. So I'd write the plan down and ask Imran to check on me.

say: Five years is better, but we still need **a plan** from somebody.
I'd tell friends **not to wait**, even though I might wait myself.
think: It gives me **breathing room**, and I might find a sign-off role in quality control or regulation.
I still believe my job goes, but I'm **not sure how** to move.
do: Save harder to reach **six months** and ask Meridian to fund a regulatory affairs course.
Talk to Imran about taking an **apprentice**, since his trade lasts.
feel: A dull, **heavy worry**, like a bill due in five years.
S3.quote: I'd tell myself, there's time, and then it's year four and there's no savings and no course.
fieldNote: Aisha knows her own habit of **putting things off** and builds in a check by asking Imran to hold her to it.
Five years moves her from frozen to a **plan**, but only on paper.

steps.text: Save harder to reach six months in the bank
Ask Meridian to fund a regulatory affairs course
Do evening study for a year while still home for the kids
Suggest Imran take on an apprentice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so no need to panic. At work I'd carry on and tell colleagues the world keeps moving slowly in practice. I might vote for anyone who says they have a serious plan for jobs, whichever side they're on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel almost fine. I'd be 53, the kids nearly grown, the mortgage nearly gone. Even if my job goes in 2036, it wouldn't land when it hurts most. I'd worry for Sana and Hamza more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on as normal, honestly. I'd keep the notebook, the reps, the pharmacies. I'd save, pay down the mortgage, and learn the new systems when they come in, not before. If a retraining option appeared in a few years I'd take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. It's a worry far away. If it were just me I'd say forget it for now, but with kids I think about it at night sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, is there a risk of doing nothing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is, yes. Ten years is a nice long time to do nothing. My plan would be to check in with myself every New Year. If I haven't tried one new thing in the year, that's a sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sana and Hamza?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to be good with people and good with their hands. Imran's trade is a good example. Sana is clever at maths and I'd tell her a degree is fine, but it's not a safe pass. I wouldn't scare them.

say: Ten years is a long time, so **no need to panic**.
I'd back anyone with a **serious plan** for jobs, whichever side they're on.
think: At 53 with the mortgage nearly gone, even a job loss wouldn't land when it **hurts most**.
I'd worry for **Sana and Hamza** more than for myself.
do: Keep the notebook and reps, **save**, and pay down the mortgage.
Learn new systems **when they arrive**, and take any retraining that appears.
feel: **Mostly calm**, with a worry that comes at night.
S4.quote: Ten years is a nice long time to do nothing. My plan would be to check in with myself every New Year.
fieldNote: Aisha is **calmer** because the mortgage would be nearly paid, but wants a New Year check against drifting.
Her advice for the kids is **people and hands-on skills**, with a degree as no guarantee.

steps.text: Pay extra on the mortgage each year
Learn the new ordering systems when the company brings them in
Review my own progress every New Year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years with no plan and two months saved. What would help is advance notice, courses that I can do without losing my wage, and a bank that works with us. And a clear message from someone in charge, not just rumours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I think you should ask how it feels to be the careful one at work. I'm the person who double-checks, and now that's the very thing that looks slow. I'd like it to count for something.

headlineQuote: I'm the person who double-checks, and now that's the very thing that looks slow. I'd like it to count for something.
portrait: Aisha is a **43-year-old** buyer at a health-products wholesaler, with an electrician husband, two kids and a mortgage.
She is careful, **never uses AI** and trusts her notebook, her reps and her own eyes on expiry dates.
Her household money is already tight: Imran's **seasonal income** and two months saved.
She tends to **put things off**, so in the slower pictures she plans to write things down and be held to them.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, with no plan and only two months saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Advance notice**, paid-time courses, a flexible bank and a clear message from those in charge.
